id_and_class.summary: Montero holds that consciousness is physical and causally effective, but that our concept of the physical is too incomplete to explain it. She proposes recasting the mind–body problem as the question of whether mentality can be accounted for in a world that is fundamentally nonmental, rather than fundamentally physical.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as Physical, Within an Incomplete Physics

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is part of the physical world, real and irreducible to current physical concepts, brain states, or functional roles.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Montero treats experience as ultimately physical while rejecting its reduction to brain states or functional roles. The open question, in her framing, is whether mentality is fundamentally nonmental.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not specified; Montero leaves open whether mentality is a fundamental feature of the world and asks physicalists to take a stand on it.
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Montero affirms the reality and distinctiveness of subjective experience without offering a mechanism for it.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Experience is real and irreducible to the concepts of current physics. Its apparent mystery reflects an impoverished grasp of the physical, not a nonphysical nature.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: A physical world whose nature is not yet adequately understood, and real, causally effective conscious experience within it.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Philosophical analysis of what ‘physical’ means, alongside science, with which Montero says stating a hypothesis works hand in hand.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal; mental causation; the metaphysical framing of the mind–body problem.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Montero offers no mechanism. Her principle is a reframing: replace the physical/nonphysical distinction with the mental/nonmental distinction, and ask whether mentality can be accounted for by nonmental phenomena.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Montero rejects epiphenomenalism and holds that conscious experience has causal efficacy, even if current science struggles to state it.
core_claims_and_evidence: Montero coined ‘the body problem’ for our limited understanding of what the physical is, by analogy with the hard problem of consciousness.
Consciousness may be physical without being reducible to the concepts of current physics.
Conscious experience is causally efficacious, so epiphenomenalism is false.
Framing the debate as mental versus nonmental separates naturalism from ontological claims and could make the debate clearer and even resolvable.

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Calling consciousness physical while conceding that the physical is poorly understood risks leaving physicalism with little content. Montero's call for a substantive hypothesis departs from deferential naturalism, the view that science alone settles what exists.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Montero leaves unanswered whether mentality is a fundamental feature of the world; she argues physicalists must decide this openly rather than hand it to future science.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: The view sits with non-reductive physicalism and is close to Russellian monism, though Montero rejects panpsychism.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Since Montero holds that we do not yet grasp what makes consciousness physical, the view gives no basis for deciding which artificial systems would have it.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Since experience is ultimately physical on this view, there is no separate mind to outlast the body.
